speaker_role: student reviewing his own FERPA admissions file; also relays secondhand process claims attributed to 'the Yale admissions podcast'
key_insights: Describes a process, sourced secondhand from a Yale admissions podcast, where two regional readers take notes and then a 5-person committee votes, with at least 4 votes needed to admit
The full multi-page application is condensed by each reader down to roughly a half-page to one page of notes, illustrating how much detail gets compressed during review
Teacher recommendations are described as weighed fairly heavily, with readers quoting specific descriptive language from them

Received a 'likely letter' nomination from one reader despite only average-looking numeric subscores, suggesting the essays and interview narrative carried more weight than the category ratings for this file
The alumni interview report was unusually long and detailed and highlighted personality traits and academic engagement; the applicant felt it was a strong part of his file
A reader noted that being one of few Hispanic students in his STEM magnet program required him to self-advocate, showing readers explicitly connect background context to an applicant's profile
specific_numbers_or_facts: States category ratings are on roughly a 1-9 (possibly 1-8) scale and overall rating on a 1-4 scale with +/-, per what he was told; he received a 5 on extracurriculars from both readers and an overall '2 plus' from each, per his file notes
notable_or_distinctive: The account of a 'likely nomination' not automatically translating into a guaranteed likely letter, reportedly requiring separate higher-level approval, is a distinctive procedural detail.
reliability_notes: Same genre as prior Yale/Stanford FERPA file-review videos already in the knowledge base (different applicant, new data). Process claims (committee structure, vote threshold, exact rating scale) are attributed to a podcast or other secondhand sources and explicitly hedged by the speaker as uncertain; auto-captions have some garbling on acronyms (e.g. an unclear term rendered as 'l13').
